opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the main contribution is really about sample efficiency. Systems like AlphaEvolve showed that putting a language model inside an evolutionary loop can find genuinely new programs and even improve on known mathematical results. But they often needed thousands of evaluations, which is a lot of compute and puts this kind of work out of reach for most academic labs.

With ShinkaEvolve we asked whether we could get comparable discoveries with orders of magnitude fewer samples. A few ingredients made that work.

First, parent sampling. We keep an archive of programs and choose which ones to mutate in a way that balances exploiting high performers against exploring promising but less-visited parts of the space. We also use an island model, so subpopulations can evolve somewhat independently.

Second, novelty rejection sampling. A lot of compute gets wasted when the LLM proposes something that's basically a copy of what you already have. So we embed candidate programs, check how similar they are to the existing archive, and if they're too close, we can ask an LLM judge whether the change is meaningfully novel before spending an expensive evaluation on it.

Third, adaptive model selection. Instead of fixing one LLM as the mutation operator, we use an ensemble of frontier models and treat choosing among them as a bandit problem. Models that have recently produced improvements get sampled more. Different models turn out to be good at different stages of the search, so this adaptivity matters.

Put together, on the circle packing benchmark we found a new state-of-the-art solution with only around 150 evaluations. We've also applied it to evolving agent scaffolds for math reasoning, to competitive programming tasks, and to discovering a better load-balancing loss for mixture-of-experts models.

The other big contribution, which I care a lot about, is that it's fully open source. The hope is that people can actually run this on their own problems on a modest budget and build on it. In a way, that's the point: democratizing this kind of open-ended, LLM-driven discovery.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls sample efficiency the main contribution and says ShinkaEvolve aims for comparable discoveries with orders of magnitude fewer evaluations.

r002.rationale: The candidate says fewer samples and modest budgets can let more people run LLM-driven discovery on their own problems, describing this as democratization.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the main contribution of ShinkaEvolve is sample efficiency. The whole field, with AlphaEvolve and the work that followed it, showed that you can wrap a language model in an evolutionary loop and get real discoveries out of it. But those systems are incredibly expensive. You're talking about thousands, sometimes tens of thousands of program evaluations, and each evaluation might be a long compute job. So the question we asked ourselves at Sakana was: can we get the same quality of result with maybe a hundred-and-fifty samples instead of thousands?

And the way we got there wasn't one big trick, it was three smaller ideas that compound. The first is how you pick parents. Most systems either sample uniformly from the archive or just take the best program. We do something closer to a fitness-and-novelty balanced sampling with islands, so you keep diversity but still exploit what works. The second is rejecting mutations before you ever evaluate them. We embed proposed programs and if a candidate is too similar to something already in the archive, we throw it away before spending any compute on it. That alone saves a huge fraction of wasted evaluations, because LLMs love to propose near-duplicates. And the third is a bandit over the LLMs themselves. We don't commit to one model as the mutation operator. We run several and let a UCB-style bandit learn online which model is actually producing improvements for this particular problem, because that varies a lot between tasks.

The headline result was circle packing, where we matched or slightly beat AlphaEvolve's number with roughly a hundred-and-fifty evaluations. But honestly the thing I'm more excited about is that it generalizes. We ran it on AtCoder heuristic problems, on mixture-of-experts load balancing losses, on AIME reasoning scaffolds, and it worked across all of them without tuning. And it's fully open source, which matters because the previous systems weren't. I think the contribution to the field is really saying: this doesn't have to be a Google-scale thing. An academic lab or even an individual can run this on a laptop with an API key and get meaningful discoveries.

r001.rationale: It names sample efficiency as the main contribution and explains achieving comparable results with about 150 evaluations instead of thousands.

r002.rationale: It says the approach means scientific discovery need not require Google-scale resources and that an academic lab or individual can use it with a laptop and API key.

astra-6.text:
I think the main contribution is making evolutionary search with language models more sample-efficient. A language model can propose a change to a program, but that’s only one part of the problem. You also have to decide which programs to build on, how to maintain diverse approaches, and where to spend your evaluation budget.

Shinka Evolve brings those decisions into the search loop. You generate a candidate, evaluate it, and use that feedback to guide subsequent proposals. The aim is to get more useful progress out of each expensive model call, rather than relying on a huge number of attempts.

So I’d frame it as a contribution to the search system around the language model: how do we turn its ability to propose changes into a sustained process of discovery?

r001.rationale: It describes getting more progress from each expensive model call, but does not clearly identify reducing the number of program evaluations needed to find improvements.

r002.rationale: It does not say that sample efficiency makes scientific discovery accessible to more people.

sol-6.1.text: I’d say the main contribution is making language-model-driven evolutionary search more sample-efficient. The language model proposes changes to a program, and then we evaluate those changes and use the results to guide the next round of search. The interesting question is how you organize that loop: which solutions you build on, how you maintain diversity, and how you allocate your generation budget. Shinka Evolve brings those pieces together so you can discover better programs with fewer evaluations, rather than relying on a huge number of attempts.

r001.rationale: The response calls improved sample efficiency the main contribution and says it can find better programs with fewer evaluations.

r002.rationale: It does not say that this efficiency makes LLM-driven scientific discovery accessible to more people.
